persona.name: Vijaya Deshmukh
persona.background: She works long hours with irregular meals and recently had a hospital admission for a systemic infection. Family members report a recent decline in her cognition and mood.

diagnoses.name: Myxedema Madness (severe hypothyroidism with neuropsychiatric manifestations)
diagnoses.description: Severe hypothyroidism presenting with hypothermia and neuropsychiatric manifestations such as depression; rarely in elderly, dementia/psychosis/confusion/disorientation with delusions/hallucinations; may develop shortly after starting thyroid hormone replacement.

diagnoses.name: Subclinical Hypothyroidism
diagnoses.description: Increased serum TSH with normal serum free T4; prevalent in women and elderly; can have neuropsychiatric manifestations and increased risk for Alzheimer disease.

diagnoses.name: Sick Euthyroid Syndrome/Nonthyroid Illness State (NTIS)
diagnoses.description: Thyroid function changes in systemic illness/surgery/fasting not caused by primary thyroid or pituitary dysfunction; commonly low T3; TSH usually normal; treatment with thyroxine is not recommended.

diagnoses.name: Addison’s Disease (Primary Adrenal Insufficiency)
diagnoses.description: Chronic adrenocortical insufficiency with prominent fatigue and weight loss; may have postural hypotension and salt craving; pigmentation is nearly always present in primary (not secondary).

diagnoses.name: Acute Adrenal Crisis (Addisonian Crisis)
diagnoses.description: Acute presentation with hypotension and circulatory failure/shock out of proportion to current illness, dehydration, acute abdomen, unexplained hypoglycemia, and unexplained fever.

diagnoses.name: Cushing’s Syndrome
diagnoses.description: Features include central obesity, moon face, buffalo hump, hypertension, purplish striae, bruising, proximal myopathy, glucose intolerance/diabetes, and neuropsychiatric symptoms (depression/euphoria/psychosis/irritability).

diagnoses.name: Ectopic ACTH Secretion
diagnoses.description: May cause impaired glucose tolerance (gluconeogenesis), hypokalemic alkalosis (mineralocorticoid activity of cortisol), and skin pigmentation.

diagnoses.name: Primary Hyperparathyroidism
diagnoses.description: Often asymptomatic hypercalcemia; classical symptoms include 'moans, bones, stones, abdominal groans' with psychiatric manifestations (lethargy, fatigue, depression, memory loss, confusion, stupor, coma), renal stones/polyuria/polydipsia, constipation/nausea/vomiting/peptic ulcers/pancreatitis.

diagnoses.name: Subclinical Hyperthyroidism
diagnoses.description: Normal free T4 and T3 with subnormal TSH (<0.5 mU/L); may normalize or progress; cardiac effects include resting tachycardia and atrial fibrillation; noncardiac effects include osteoporosis and increased fracture risk; may be associated with dementia.

diagnoses.name: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
diagnoses.description: Gradual onset over months to years with polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia, blurred vision, unexplained weakness or weight loss; often detected on routine blood/urine testing; can present with chronic complications.

initialComplaint: “I’ve been feeling very low and confused lately, and my family says I’m not myself. I also feel unusually cold.”
medicalHistory: Recent hospitalization for systemic illness (infection) with poor oral intake. Family reports she recently started thyroid hormone replacement and soon after developed worsening confusion.
symptoms:
Hypothermia with neuropsychiatric manifestations: depression; in an elderly patient with severe hypothyroidism she has become confused and disoriented with striking hallucinations and delusions. Symptoms began shortly after starting thyroid hormone replacement.

idealPathway.diseaseName: Myxedema Madness (severe hypothyroidism with neuropsychiatric manifestations)

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about feeling unusually cold and/or documented low body temperature (hypothermia).
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: Myxedema madness presents with hypothermia and is a key hallmark of severe hypothyroid decompensation.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: History of feeling unusually cold or noted low temperature consistent with hypothermia.
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “Myxedema Madness: Patient presents with hypothermia and neuropsychiatric manifestations.”

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about neuropsychiatric symptoms: depression, confusion, disorientation, dementia, psychosis, delusions, hallucinations.
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: Neuropsychiatric manifestations define myxedema madness and can range from depression to frank psychosis/dementia, especially in elderly patients with severe hypothyroidism.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: Depression or (rarely) frank dementia/psychosis with confusion, disorientation, delusions and hallucinations.
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “Rarely, elderly patient with severe hypothyroidism may become frankly demented, psychotic, confused, disoriented, sometimes with striking delusions and hallucinations.”

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about recent initiation of thyroid hormone (T4) replacement and timing of symptom onset after starting therapy.
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: Myxedema madness may develop shortly after starting T4 replacement, so temporal association helps support the diagnosis and avoid misattribution to primary psychiatric illness.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: Neuropsychiatric symptoms developing shortly after starting T4 replacement.
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “It may develop shortly after starting T4 replacement.”

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about symptoms/signs of hypothyroidism: lethargy/somnolence, weight gain, cold intolerance, hoarse voice, cognitive dysfunction, constipation, depression/psychosis.
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: Myxedema madness occurs in the context of severe hypothyroidism; eliciting broader hypothyroid symptom burden supports the underlying endocrine diagnosis.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: Multiple hypothyroid symptoms (e.g., lethargy/somnolence, weight gain, cold intolerance, cognitive dysfunction, constipation, depression/psychosis).
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “Clinical features of hypothyroidism… Lethargy, somnolence, weight gain… Cold intolerance… cognitive dysfunction… constipation… depression, psychosis.”

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about possible precipitating illness/events and drug exposures in a poorly controlled hypothyroid patient (infection, myocardial infarction, hypothermia, surgery; drugs such as amiodarone, β-blockers, diuretics, anesthetic agents, barbiturates, lithium, narcotics, phenothiazines).
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: Severe hypothyroid decompensation can be precipitated by acute events or drugs; identifying these supports diagnosis and guides evaluation for triggers.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: Recent precipitating event/illness or exposure to listed drugs.
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “It can be precipitated by an acute event… such as infection, myocardial infarction, hypothermia, surgery, drugs (amiodarone, β-blockers… lithium, narcotics, and phenothiazines)…”

keyExaminations.action: Measure core temperature and assess for cool, pale skin.
keyExaminations.reasoning: Hypothermia is central to myxedema coma/madness; cool pale skin is a warning sign in severe hypothyroid decompensation.
keyExaminations.textbookReference: “Warning signs: Presence of cool pale skin (due to hypothermia—body temperature may be as low as 25°C)”

keyExaminations.action: Perform a focused mental status examination for altered sensorium and neuropsychiatric features (confusion, disorientation, psychosis).
keyExaminations.reasoning: Myxedema madness is characterized by neuropsychiatric manifestations and may overlap with decreased mentation seen in severe hypothyroidism.
keyExaminations.expectedFinding: Altered sensorium and/or confusion, disorientation, psychosis.
keyExaminations.textbookReference: “Myxedema Madness… neuropsychiatric manifestations… confused, disoriented… delusions and hallucinations.”

keyExaminations.action: Assess cardiovascular status for bradycardia and hypotension.
keyExaminations.reasoning: Severe hypothyroidism/myxedema decompensation is associated with bradycardia and hypotension, supporting severity assessment.

keyExaminations.action: Examine for myxedema facies and nonpitting edema (hands/feet/eyelids), including periorbital puffiness.
keyExaminations.reasoning: Myxedema (nonpitting edema) and myxedema facies support the diagnosis of severe hypothyroidism.
keyExaminations.expectedFinding: Nonpitting edema of hands/feet/eyelids and/or myxedema facies (periorbital puffiness, scanty eyebrows, facial pallor/lemon-yellow tint, purplish lips, malar flush).
keyExaminations.textbookReference: “Myxedema (nonpitting edema of the skin of hands, feet and eyelids)… Myxedema facies… striking periorbital puffiness… purplish lips and malar flush.”

keyInvestigations.reasoning: TSH is the investigation of choice for hypothyroidism; high TSH supports primary hypothyroidism underlying myxedema madness.
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: High serum TSH (usually high; sometimes only slightly elevated in severe decompensation).
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “Serum TSH: It is the investigation of choice. High TSH level confirms primary hypothyroidism.”

keyInvestigations.reasoning: Free T4 confirms hypothyroid state and is specifically noted to be low in myxedema coma (severe hypothyroidism).

keyInvestigations.action: Order serum sodium and blood glucose (RBS).
keyInvestigations.reasoning: Myxedema madness is associated with hyponatremia and hypoglycemia; these also indicate severity and need urgent correction.
CPK is increased in myxedema madness and is often markedly raised in severe hypothyroidism.

keyInvestigations.action: Order ECG and arterial blood gases (ABG).
keyInvestigations.reasoning: Myxedema madness can show reduced ECG voltage; blood gases often reveal respiratory acidosis with hypoxia and hypercapnia, supporting diagnosis and severity (hypoventilation).
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: ECG: reduced voltage; ABG: respiratory acidosis with hypoxia and hypercapnia.
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “Reduced ECG voltage, blood gases often reveal respiratory acidosis, hypoxia and hypercapnia.”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Myxedema coma (severe hypothyroidism with decreased mentation)
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Assess for hallmark features of myxedema coma (decreased mentation and hypothermia) and other systemic features (bradycardia, hypotension, hypoventilation, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia). Myxedema madness emphasizes hypothermia with neuropsychiatric manifestations (depression to psychosis/dementia).
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “The hallmarks of myxedema coma are decreased mentation and hypothermia… Myxedema Madness: Patient presents with hypothermia and neuropsychiatric manifestations.”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Sick euthyroid syndrome / Nonthyroid illness state (NTIS)
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Consider systemic illness/surgery/fasting context; thyroid tests may show variable T4 and usually normal TSH influenced by illness; treatment with thyroxine is not recommended (unlike true hypothyroidism).
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Changes in thyroid function in the setting of systemic illness… referred to as the nonthyroidal illness syndrome… Serum TSH is usually normal… Treatment with thyroxine is not recommended.”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Subclinical hypothyroidism
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Check thyroid function tests: subclinical hypothyroidism has increased TSH with normal free T4; myxedema madness implies severe hypothyroidism with low free T4 and systemic/lab derangements (e.g., hypothermia, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia).
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Subclinical hypothyroidism is defined as an increased serum TSH in the presence of a normal serum free T4.”

idealPathway.diagnosticApproach: Suspect myxedema madness in an older patient presenting with hypothermia plus neuropsychiatric manifestations (depression; rarely dementia/psychosis with confusion, disorientation, delusions/hallucinations), including cases occurring shortly after starting T4 replacement. Perform focused examination for hypothermia (cool pale skin), altered sensorium, and supportive severe hypothyroid signs (bradycardia, hypotension, nonpitting edema/myxedema facies). Order cost-effective tests first: serum TSH (investigation of choice) and free T4 to confirm hypothyroidism, then screen for typical associated abnormalities (serum sodium and blood glucose; CPK). Use ECG and ABG to identify reduced voltage and respiratory acidosis/hypoxia/hypercapnia. Differentiate from NTIS (systemic illness with usually normal TSH; thyroxine not recommended) and from subclinical hypothyroidism (normal free T4).

precomputedExplanations.diagnosisName: Myxedema Madness (severe hypothyroidism with neuropsychiatric manifestations)
precomputedExplanations.description: Myxedema madness is a neuropsychiatric presentation of severe **hypothyroidism**, often in older adults, characterized by hypothermia and prominent mental status changes. It can include depression, confusion, disorientation, and sometimes frank psychosis with **delusions** and **hallucinations**, and may appear shortly after starting **thyroid hormone replacement**.
keySymptoms: **Hypothermia** - Reflects reduced metabolic heat production in severe hypothyroidism; signals life-threatening decompensation.
**Depression** - Common hypothyroid manifestation; supports endocrine cause of mood symptoms rather than primary psychiatry.
**Confusion and disorientation** - Indicates encephalopathy from severe hypothyroidism, often worsening in elderly patients.
**Hallucinations and delusions** - Psychotic features can occur in myxedema madness, distinguishing it from simple depression.
**Symptoms after starting thyroid replacement** - Myxedema madness may emerge shortly after **T4/T3** initiation, matching classic timing.
**Hyponatremia** - Due to impaired free-water clearance/ADH dysregulation in hypothyroidism; contributes to confusion.
**Hypoglycemia** - Reduced gluconeogenesis and slowed metabolism in severe hypothyroidism; worsens neurocognitive symptoms.
**Hypercapnia and hypoxia** - Hypoventilation from hypothyroid respiratory drive depression causes CO2 retention and encephalopathy.
**Increased CO2/respiratory acidosis** - Supports hypoventilation physiology typical of severe hypothyroidism-related respiratory failure.
**Elevated CPK** - Suggests hypothyroid myopathy/rhabdomyolysis tendency; supportive lab clue in severe hypothyroidism.
**Low-voltage ECG** - Classic supportive finding in myxedema (often with effusions/edema), reinforcing severe hypothyroid state.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: The patient’s hypothermia plus prominent neuropsychiatric changes (depression progressing to confusion, disorientation, hallucinations, and delusions) strongly matches **myxedema madness**, a severe **hypothyroidism** presentation seen especially in older adults. The timing—symptoms beginning shortly after starting **thyroid hormone replacement**—is specifically described in this condition. Supporting laboratory and physiologic findings (hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, hypercapnia with respiratory acidosis/hypoxia, elevated CPK, and low-voltage ECG) align with severe hypothyroid decompensation. Together, these features make myxedema madness the best unifying diagnosis over primary psychiatric disease or isolated delirium.

precomputedExplanations.description: **Subclinical hypothyroidism** is mild thyroid failure defined by elevated **TSH** with normal free **T4**. Many patients are asymptomatic or have subtle, nonspecific symptoms and do not develop severe systemic decompensation.
keySymptoms: **Mild fatigue** - Low energy without major cognitive impairment or psychosis; often intermittent and nonspecific.
**Weight gain** - Small, gradual increase in weight due to reduced metabolic rate; not rapid or profound.
**Cold intolerance** - Feeling colder than others, typically mild; not associated with **hypothermia**.
**Constipation** - Slower bowel movements, usually manageable; not accompanied by severe metabolic derangements.
**Dry skin** - Coarse, dry skin changes that develop slowly; not a marker of acute decompensation.
**Menstrual changes** - Irregular or heavy menses may occur; less relevant postmenopausally in older adults.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: This patient has **hypothermia** with prominent **neuropsychiatric manifestations** (confusion, disorientation, hallucinations, delusions) and multiple laboratory/physiologic abnormalities (e.g., **hyponatremia**, **hypoglycemia**, hypercapnia/respiratory acidosis, elevated **CPK**, low-voltage ECG). These findings indicate severe, systemic hypothyroid decompensation rather than a mild biochemical abnormality. The timing—symptoms beginning shortly after starting thyroid hormone replacement—is a classic association described with **myxedema madness**. Therefore, labeling this as **subclinical hypothyroidism** does not match the severity or pattern of illness.
precomputedExplanations.whyIncorrectForCase: **Subclinical hypothyroidism** typically has normal free **T4** and does not cause **hypothermia**, psychosis, or respiratory failure physiology. This patient’s profound mental status changes plus multisystem abnormalities are far more consistent with **myxedema madness** from severe hypothyroidism.
keyDifferencesFromCorrect: **Severity of thyroid dysfunction** - Subclinical: elevated **TSH** with normal **T4**; Myxedema madness: severe hypothyroidism with systemic decompensation.
**Mental status** - Subclinical: none or mild cognitive slowing; Myxedema madness: **confusion**, **disorientation**, **delusions**, **hallucinations**.
**Temperature regulation** - Subclinical: mild cold intolerance; Myxedema madness: true **hypothermia**.
**Metabolic labs** - Subclinical: usually normal sodium/glucose; Myxedema madness: **hyponatremia** and **hypoglycemia** are characteristic.
**Respiratory physiology** - Subclinical: no ventilatory failure; Myxedema madness: **hypoventilation** with **hypercapnia** and **respiratory acidosis**.
**Cardiac/other markers** - Subclinical: typically no low-voltage ECG or marked **CPK** rise; Myxedema madness: reduced ECG voltage and elevated **CPK** can occur.
**Treatment relationship** - Subclinical: symptoms not classically triggered by starting therapy; Myxedema madness: may develop shortly after initiating **thyroid hormone replacement**.
missingFindings: **Normal free T4** - Required for subclinical hypothyroidism; severe systemic features suggest low **T4** instead.
**Absence of severe systemic decompensation** - Subclinical disease should not produce **hypothermia**, psychosis, or respiratory acidosis.
**Stable electrolytes and glucose** - Subclinical hypothyroidism usually lacks **hyponatremia** and **hypoglycemia** seen here.

precomputedExplanations.description: **Sick Euthyroid Syndrome (NTIS)** is an adaptive alteration in thyroid hormone levels during acute or chronic systemic illness without intrinsic thyroid gland failure. Typical patterns include low **T3** (± low **T4**) with **TSH** that is low/normal early and may rise slightly during recovery, and treatment is usually supportive rather than thyroid hormone replacement.
keySymptoms: **Systemic illness context** - Occurs during severe infection, trauma, surgery, or organ failure causing thyroid test changes.
**Low T3 symptoms absent** - Patients usually lack classic hypothyroid signs; symptoms reflect underlying illness instead.
**No primary thyroid failure** - Clinical picture is dominated by critical illness, not progressive hypothyroid features.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: NTIS is primarily a laboratory phenomenon seen in significant non-thyroidal systemic illness, with thyroid tests altered by cytokines, reduced peripheral conversion of **T4 to T3**, and changes in binding proteins. It does not typically produce profound **hypothermia** or prominent neuropsychiatric syndromes as a primary manifestation. In this case, the patient has features consistent with severe hypothyroidism physiology (e.g., **hyponatremia**, **hypoglycemia**, **hypercapnia/respiratory acidosis**, low-voltage ECG) and a classic neuropsychiatric presentation. The timing shortly after starting thyroid hormone replacement is also described with **myxedema madness**, not NTIS.
precomputedExplanations.whyIncorrectForCase: This patient’s presentation is driven by severe hypothyroidism with **hypothermia** and frank **psychosis/confusion**, which is not typical for NTIS. NTIS would be expected in the setting of a major systemic illness and usually lacks striking hypothyroid clinical signs and the characteristic severe hypothyroid lab/physiology pattern seen here.
keyDifferencesFromCorrect: **Primary process** - NTIS is thyroid test alteration from illness; **myxedema madness** is true severe hypothyroidism with CNS effects.
**Temperature** - NTIS does not usually cause marked **hypothermia**; myxedema states commonly present with **hypothermia**.
**Neuropsychiatric profile** - NTIS rarely causes primary **delusions/hallucinations**; myxedema can cause **psychosis/delirium**.
**Electrolytes/glucose** - NTIS has variable labs; myxedema commonly shows **hyponatremia** and **hypoglycemia**.
**Ventilation/ABG** - NTIS does not classically cause **hypercapnic respiratory acidosis**; myxedema can cause hypoventilation with **hypercapnia**.
**Trigger with thyroid replacement** - NTIS is not characteristically precipitated after starting thyroid hormone; myxedema madness may develop shortly after **T replacement**.
missingFindings: **Severe systemic non-thyroidal illness** - Lack of a clear precipitating critical illness makes NTIS unlikely as primary diagnosis.
**Typical NTIS thyroid pattern** - Expected low **T3** with low/normal **TSH** (± low **T4**) is not provided and would be needed.
**Absence of classic hypothyroid physiology** - Presence of **hypothermia**, **hyponatremia**, **hypoglycemia**, and **hypercapnia** argues against NTIS.

precomputedExplanations.description: Addison’s disease is **primary adrenal insufficiency** due to destruction or dysfunction of the adrenal cortex, causing deficient **cortisol** and often **aldosterone**. It typically presents with chronic fatigue, weight loss, **orthostatic hypotension**, and characteristic **hyperpigmentation**, and can decompensate into an **adrenal crisis** during stress.
keySymptoms: **Fatigue/weakness** - Progressive low energy from **cortisol deficiency** and impaired stress response.
**Weight loss/anorexia** - Chronic catabolic state and reduced appetite in untreated adrenal insufficiency.
**Orthostatic hypotension** - **Aldosterone deficiency** causes salt wasting, volume depletion, and postural dizziness.
**Hyperpigmentation** - Elevated **ACTH** increases melanocyte stimulation, darkening skin and mucosa.
**GI symptoms** - Nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain may occur, especially in adrenal crisis.
**Salt craving** - Compensatory behavior from chronic sodium loss due to mineralocorticoid deficiency.
**Hyperkalemia** - Reduced renal potassium excretion from low **aldosterone** (primary, not secondary).
**Hyponatremia** - Salt wasting and increased **ADH** can lower serum sodium levels.
**Hypoglycemia** - Low **cortisol** impairs gluconeogenesis, especially in fasting or illness.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: This patient’s dominant syndrome is hypothermia with prominent **neuropsychiatric manifestations** (depression, confusion, disorientation, hallucinations/delusions) occurring shortly after starting **thyroid hormone replacement**, which is classic for **Myxedema Madness** (severe hypothyroidism with psychosis). While Addison’s can cause **hyponatremia** and **hypoglycemia**, it does not characteristically cause hypothermia with severe psychosis temporally linked to thyroid replacement. The provided supportive data—**increased CO2**, **respiratory acidosis with hypoxia/hypercapnia**, **elevated CPK**, low-voltage ECG, slow-wave EEG, and elevated CSF protein—align far more strongly with severe hypothyroidism than with primary adrenal failure.
precomputedExplanations.whyIncorrectForCase: Addison’s disease typically features **hyperpigmentation**, **hyperkalemia**, and **hypotension/volume depletion**, none of which are described in this case. The hallmark clue here is psychosis/confusion developing shortly after **thyroid replacement** in an elderly patient with severe hypothyroidism—classic for **Myxedema Madness**, not Addison’s.
keyDifferencesFromCorrect: **Trigger/temporal pattern** - Addison’s worsens with physiologic stress; **Myxedema Madness** may appear after starting **T4/T3**.
**Temperature regulation** - Addison’s is not classically hypothermic; severe hypothyroidism often causes **hypothermia**.
**Electrolytes** - Addison’s commonly causes **hyperkalemia**; **Myxedema Madness** more often shows **hyponatremia** without hyperkalemia.
**Cardiorespiratory findings** - Addison’s does not cause **hypercapnic respiratory acidosis**; hypothyroidism can cause hypoventilation with **CO2 retention**.
**Cardiac testing** - Addison’s lacks typical low-voltage ECG; hypothyroidism can show **reduced voltage** and bradycardic features.
**Muscle enzymes** - Addison’s does not typically raise **CPK**; hypothyroidism often increases **CPK** from myopathy.
**Neuropsychiatric profile** - Addison’s may cause fatigue/apathy; **Myxedema Madness** can cause frank **psychosis** with hallucinations/delusions.
missingFindings: **Hyperpigmentation** - Absence of ACTH-driven skin/mucosal darkening makes primary adrenal failure unlikely.
**Hyperkalemia** - Not reported; primary adrenal insufficiency usually elevates potassium via low **aldosterone**.
**Orthostatic hypotension/shock** - No postural symptoms or hemodynamic collapse described, expected in Addison’s/adrenal crisis.
**Volume depletion/dehydration** - Not mentioned; Addison’s typically causes salt wasting and dehydration.
**Eosinophilia** - Often present in adrenal insufficiency; not provided among case labs.
**Autoimmune context** - No history of autoimmune disease (e.g., autoimmune thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes) suggesting polyglandular syndrome.

precomputedExplanations.description: An **acute adrenal crisis** is a life-threatening state of **cortisol deficiency** (often with **aldosterone deficiency**) causing shock, electrolyte derangements, and hypoglycemia. It is typically triggered by infection, surgery, trauma, or abrupt steroid withdrawal in patients with known or unrecognized adrenal insufficiency.
keySymptoms: **Refractory hypotension/shock** - Profound low blood pressure unresponsive to fluids due to cortisol and aldosterone deficiency.
**Severe weakness/fatigue** - Marked asthenia from glucocorticoid deficiency and volume depletion.
**Nausea/vomiting/abdominal pain** - Prominent GI symptoms that can mimic an acute abdomen.
**Fever** - Common trigger-related finding, especially with infection precipitating crisis.
**Altered mental status** - Confusion, lethargy, or coma from hypoglycemia, hypotension, and metabolic disturbance.
**Hypoglycemia** - Low glucose due to impaired gluconeogenesis from cortisol deficiency.
**Hyperkalemia** - Elevated potassium from mineralocorticoid deficiency (primary adrenal insufficiency).
**Hyponatremia** - Low sodium from aldosterone loss and increased ADH driven by cortisol deficiency.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: This patient has **hypothermia** with prominent **neuropsychiatric symptoms** (depression, confusion, hallucinations/delusions) and a pattern of labs described for severe hypothyroidism (e.g., **increased CO2**, **respiratory acidosis with hypercapnia**, **elevated CPK**, **low-voltage ECG**). While **hyponatremia** and **hypoglycemia** can occur in adrenal crisis, the overall syndrome is dominated by findings classic for **myxedema-related** hypoventilation and metabolic slowing. Additionally, symptoms began shortly after starting **thyroid hormone replacement**, which is a known setting for **Myxedema Madness** rather than a primary presentation of adrenal crisis.

The hallmark combination here—**hypothermia**, **psychosis/delirium**, **hypoventilation with hypercapnia**, **elevated CPK**, and **low-voltage ECG**—fits **Myxedema Madness** far better than adrenal crisis.
keyDifferencesFromCorrect: **Temperature pattern** - Adrenal crisis often has **fever** (triggered by infection); **Myxedema Madness** features **hypothermia**.
**Respiratory findings** - Adrenal crisis does not classically cause **hypoventilation with hypercapnia**; severe hypothyroidism can cause **CO2 retention** and **respiratory acidosis**.
**Cardiac/EKG clues** - Adrenal crisis is not defined by **low-voltage ECG**; myxedema can show **reduced voltage** and bradycardic physiology.
**Muscle enzymes** - **Elevated CPK** is typical in hypothyroidism; it is not a defining feature of adrenal crisis.

**Neuropsychiatric signature** - **Delusions/hallucinations** shortly after starting **T replacement** is described in **Myxedema Madness**; adrenal crisis more often causes nonspecific lethargy/confusion from shock/hypoglycemia.

precomputedExplanations.description: Cushing’s syndrome is a state of chronic **glucocorticoid excess** from exogenous steroids or endogenous cortisol overproduction. It classically causes progressive metabolic, cardiovascular, skin, and musculoskeletal changes, often with mood disturbance rather than hypothermic delirium.
keySymptoms: **Central obesity** - Truncal weight gain with relatively thin limbs due to cortisol-driven fat redistribution.
**Moon facies** - Rounded, plethoric face from fat deposition and fluid retention.
**Dorsocervical fat pad** - "Buffalo hump" from abnormal fat accumulation over upper back and neck.
**Purple striae** - Wide violaceous abdominal striae from dermal collagen breakdown and skin thinning.
**Proximal muscle weakness** - Difficulty rising from chair or climbing stairs due to steroid myopathy.
**Hypertension** - Cortisol increases vascular tone and mineralocorticoid activity, raising blood pressure chronically.
**Hyperglycemia** - Increased gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance leading to diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance.
**Easy bruising** - Skin and vessel fragility from protein catabolism and impaired connective tissue integrity.
**Osteoporosis** - Bone loss and fractures from inhibited osteoblast function and calcium imbalance.
**Mood changes** - Depression, irritability, or insomnia; frank psychosis can occur but is less typical.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: The target diagnosis would be considered when a patient has signs of **hypercortisolism** such as truncal obesity, **purple striae**, **proximal myopathy**, **hypertension**, and **hyperglycemia**. Neuropsychiatric symptoms can occur in Cushing’s, but they usually accompany systemic cushingoid features rather than presenting with **hypothermia**.
